chunks: Where are the Amalekites and the sons of the Amalekites!
Where are the Pharaohs and the sons of the Pharaohs!
Where are the people of the cities of ar-Rass who killed the prophets, extinguished the traditions of the divine messengers, and revived the traditions of the despots!
Where are those who advanced with armies, defeated thousands, mobilized forces, and populated cities?!

key_terms.السُّنَنَ: The traditions or customs (of the prophets or despots)
key_terms.الْعَمَالِقَةُ: The Amalekites, a biblical/Quranic tribe known for opposing the Israelites
key_terms.الْفَرَاعِنَةُ: The Pharaohs, plural of Pharaoh, representing Egyptian royalty and power
key_terms.مَدَائِنِ الرَّسِّ: The cities of ar-Rass, mentioned in the Quran as the dwelling place of the tribe of Hud

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the rhetorical question 'Where are...' in Nahj al-Balagha's lesson on history?
ai.summary: In this passage from Nahj al-Balagha, Imam Ali (AS) employs a series of rhetorical questions to highlight the transience of worldly power, referencing specific Quranic archetypes of tyranny such as the Amalekites, Pharaohs, and the people of ar-Rass. This serves as a profound lesson for the era of the Mahdi (AJ), reminding believers that the grandeur of empires and their military might are ultimately fleeting, urging them to focus on spiritual endurance rather than temporal dominance. The invocation of these groups underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on the cyclical nature of divine justice and the inevitable fall of the oppressors.
